newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No easy solution seen to Russian economic woes.
newsitem.headline: No easy solution seen to Russian economic woes.

text.p: Cabinet changes planned by President Boris Yeltsin will aim to ease the hardships facing millions of Russians, but analysts said on Wednesday there was little chance of a quick and painless economic fix.

Russian ministers, their economy battered by five years of market reforms, are struggling to unravel a web of wage and payments arrears which have left many workers and pensioners living below the poverty line.

Tax revenues remain stubbornly low and the International Monetary Fund, annoyed at Russia's inability to meet ambitious budget plans, is set to delay handing over the latest tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan.

"There is no miracle solution, and it is going to be very bloody," said Christopher Granville, chief economist at United City Bank in Moscow. "The crisis in public finances has deep structural causes."
Yeltsin, returning to the political fray after a long absence through illness, highlighted Russia's social problems this week and hinted a government reshuffle was on the cards.
"Maybe we need some changes, maybe we need some names, maybe we need some people to be changed in the government," he told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in remarks broadcast on television.

"An opinion poll showed that most Russians were unhappy with the government, the premier and the president... The main thing is that the government cannot cope with (delayed) pensions, wages and payments."
Newspapers speculated -- not for the first time -- that Chernomyrdin himself could be on the way out, but the Kremlin has denied that this is the case.

Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday that the planned government changes would aim to deepen economic reforms. "We have to roll up sleeves and get down to hard work... We have to work at the microeconomic level," he said.
Izvestia newspaper on Wednesday tipped reformers Anatoly Chubais and Yegor Gaidar for roles in a reshuffled government.

Both are bitterly unpopular with Russia's conservative parliament and while Chubais is currently playing a big political role as Yeltsin's chief of staff, the Kremlin gave no signs of being ready to summon back Gaidar, an economist with no strong political base or public backing.

Gaidar, 40, launched Russia's first radical pro-market reform programme in 1992, but his reformist party failed to muster enough votes to win seats in the lower house of parliament in elections held in December 1995.

Jeffrey Sachs, Director of the Harvard Institute for International Development and a one-time adviser to the Russian government, told Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday that he was unhappy with the way Russia was governed.
"The government in the last few years has spent much too much time figuring who is going to pocket what assets and much too little thinking about how to balance the books," he said.

"The government has given away vast amounts of natural resources and ended up quite short in terms of paying the basic bills like pensions... I do not think Russia has been properly governed in recent years."
Sachs said there were signs of an economic turnaround after years of decline, but he added:

"Hyperinflation has been broken but it has been broken in a context which has created massive inequalities of wealth, enormous cynicism and enormous corruption. Russia has a lot of cleaning up to do to become a normal country."
